title: Ceviche
subtitle: lime-cured raw fish with chilli and coriander
excerpt: Fresh raw fish cut into small pieces and cured in lime juice until opaque. Chilli, coriander, and tomato go in with it. This is a light, fresh dish with bold flavour -- no heat needed.
sourceNotes: Ceviche is the national dish of Peru, though versions appear across Latin America. The lime-acid cure is a Central and South American technique that predates European contact. Peru's ceviche is made quickly, with a short cure and the juice drunk as a shot.

content.text: Use the freshest fish you can find. Sashimi-grade or day-boat fish is ideal. The lime juice does not cook the fish in the same way heat does -- it changes the protein structure but the fish is still raw in spirit. Only use fish you would eat raw.

items.prepNote: very fresh, skin removed, cut into 1cm cubes
use juice of 6 limes -- the acid will cure the fish
or 1 fresh red chilli, thinly sliced
use a handful of fresh coriander leaves

content.text: Place the fish cubes in a glass or ceramic bowl. Pour over the lime juice. Stir gently.
Cover and refrigerate for 20 to 30 minutes. The fish will turn opaque as the acid firms it up.
Add the onion, spring onion, chilli, tomato, coriander, and salt. Toss gently.
Taste and adjust the salt and lime. Serve immediately, cold.

items.fix: Ceviche does not improve with a longer cure. 20 to 30 minutes is enough. Beyond an hour, the texture deteriorates.
Salt is critical here -- add it generously and taste. More lime brightens the whole dish.

items.symptom: Fish still looks raw and translucent after 30 minutes
items.cause: Not enough lime juice or fish pieces too large
items.fix: Use enough juice to completely submerge the fish. Cut pieces to no more than 1cm cubes.

content.text: Ceviche is the national dish of Peru and a source of great pride. Versions of it appear across Latin America, but Peru's style -- fresh, quick-cured, and served with its lime juice -- is widely considered the definitive form. The dish has pre-Columbian roots and has been made along Peru's Pacific coast for thousands of years. Today it is one of the most celebrated dishes in world cooking.
